You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details: The test case creates an instance of FDistributionImpl with numerator and denominator degrees of freedom both set to 1.0 and performs cumulativeProbability and inverseCumulativeProbability calls. The reported issue references an IllegalArgumentException related to denominatorDegreeOfFreedom in FDistribution leading to errors in a root bracketing utility, especially noticeable with denominator degrees of freedom equal to 2.

Looking at the constructor FDistributionImpl(double numeratorDegreesOfFreedom, double denominatorDegreesOfFreedom), it simply calls setter methods for the numerator and denominator degrees of freedom.

The setter for denominatorDegreesOfFreedom requires the degree of freedom to be positive, which 2.0 satisfies, so no exception arises there.

The cumulativeProbability method calculates the cumulative probability using the Beta regularized function, with arguments dependent on numerator and denominator degrees of freedom and the input x.

The inverseCumulativeProbability method has boundary checks for p = 0 or 1 and otherwise delegates to the superclass method inverseCumulativeProbability.

The root cause hinted by the bug report is that for specific denominators like 2, the internal solver (UnivariateRealSolverUtils.bracket) used in inverse cumulative probability calculation encounters values or ranges that lead to IllegalArgumentException.

The F-distribution's cumulativeProbability relies on the Beta regularized function with formula (n * x) / (m + n * x) for numerator n and denominator m degrees of freedom. When degrees of freedom are small (e.g., 1 or 2), this formula can involve values causing difficulty for numerical solvers in the inverse calculation step.

The failure likely comes from the inverseCumulativeProbability method inherited behavior (superclass call), which calls a root solver that attempts to bracket the root for the inverse function. The solver can fail if the function shape or bracketing interval is incorrect or not appropriate due to small degrees of freedom values.

Thus, the bug occurs because the inverseCumulativeProbability in FDistributionImpl relies on a root-finder that assumes behavior or intervals that do not hold for small denominator degrees of freedom such as 2, leading to IllegalArgumentExceptions.

No evidence suggests a missing check or incorrect degree of freedom validation. Instead, the issue likely lies in the interaction of small denominator degrees of freedom with the inverse cumulative probability solver.

Hence, the problematic area is the method inverseCumulativeProbability and potentially the superclass method it delegates to, as well as possible interplay with the root-finding utilities.

Recent bug reports related to UnivariateRealSolver are not directly addressing similar parameter-dependent bracketing problems, so they provide little additional evidence.

The fix should investigate introducing safeguards, improved initial bracketing, or special-case handling in the inverseCumulativeProbability method or its underlying root-finder calls for small denominator degrees of freedom cases.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
